claims.claim: A backup is a separate, recoverable copy of data that lets you restore after loss from causes such as hardware failure, theft, accidental deletion, and ransomware.
The 3-2-1 rule keeps three copies of important data, on two different types of storage media, with one copy stored offsite.
Backups should be tested so a team can rapidly restore data both fully and partially; regular backups protect against ransomware, malware, hardware failures, and physical damage.
Many ransomware variants attempt to find and subsequently delete or encrypt accessible backups, so backups should be maintained offline and encrypted (or immutable), and tested regularly.

A full backup captures all selected files; an incremental backup captures files created or changed since the last backup of any type; a differential backup stores files created or modified since the last full backup.

Recovering from an incremental backup may require media from the last full backup plus each subsequent incremental, whereas a differential restore needs only the last full backup and the most recent differential.
It is good practice to store backed-up data offsite so data is protected from threatening elements at the primary location.
File synchronization keeps copies identical, so a deletion or ransomware encryption propagates to synced copies; a separate, ideally offline backup is safer than relying on sync alone.
claims.note: Reasoned from CISA's point that ransomware deletes/encrypts accessible backups and its recommendation to keep offline copies; sync mirrors changes to reachable copies, so it shares that exposure.

sourceRecords.title: Back Up Business Data
sourceRecords.notes: Read via curl with a browser user-agent (WebFetch returned 403). States the 3-2-1 rule verbatim: '3 copies of important files, 2 different types of storage media (like a hard drive and the cloud), 1 copy stored off-site.' Also supports: regular backups protect against ransomware, malware, hardware failures and physical damage; use a combination of on-site and remote backups; leverage offline copies and encryption; and 'Test backup procedure to make sure your team can rapidly restore data both fully and partially.' Used for the 3-2-1 rule, reasons to back up, and testing-restore guidance.

sourceRecords.title: #StopRansomware Guide (September 2023)
sourceRecords.provider: CISA, FBI, NSA, and MS-ISAC (joint guide, hosted by CISA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via curl with a browser user-agent (WebFetch returned 403). Supports: 'Maintain offline, encrypted backups of critical data, and regularly test the availability and integrity of backups'; 'It is important that backups are maintained offline, as many ransomware variants attempt to find and subsequently delete or encrypt accessible backups to make restoration impossible unless the ransom is paid'; and that some cloud vendors offer immutable storage solutions. Used for the offline/immutable-copy point and the sync/connected-copy exposure to ransomware.

sourceRecords.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sourceRecords.notes: Downloaded the PDF and extracted text with pypdf. May 2010, by Marianne Swanson et al. Section 5 defines the three common backup methods: 'Full. A full backup captures all files on the disk or within the folder selected for backup.' 'Incremental. An incremental backup captures files that were created or changed since the last backup, regardless of backup type.' 'Differential. A differential backup stores files that were created or modified since the last full backup.' Section 3.4.2 states 'It is good business practice to store backed-up data offsite.' Used for backup-type definitions, their restore trade-offs, and offsite storage practice.
